messages.subject: planting milkweed
messages.text:
Hello, 

 

 
I'd like to purchase milkweed seeds but I'm very confused as how to plant them.

 

 
In your guidelines it says to plant in May >, but it also says it's essential to plant them before the last frost. The last frost is usually in April (I'm in TN). It also says to stratify the seeds in the refrigerator in an airtight container, but then to
 plant the "bombs" in with space between them. Later it says to plant the "can".

 

 
Can you explain what bombs and cans are, and which one to use?

 

 
Thanks in advance for your clarification!

 

 
ginger lyvere peck

messages.subject: Re: planting milkweed
messages.text:
Hi Ginger,

This reply is coming far too late, you wrote back in March and it's now July. That's not how we do things here, and I'm sorry. Let me finally answer your question, because it's a good one.

We sell milkweed in two forms:

- Seed packets: loose seeds you cold-stratify yourself in the fridge for about 30 days before planting.
- Seed bombs: small clay balls with seeds already mixed into compost and clay, and the cold stratification is already done for you.

So the "bombs" and the "can" in the guide are the same thing (seed bombs), just worded inconsistently. There's no separate "can" product, sorry for the confusion.

In Tennessee, with your last frost usually in April, you're in a great spot. Here's what I'd suggest:

If you go with seed bombs: plant them directly in the ground in April, just after your last frost. Press them lightly into the soil, no more than 5 mm deep, barely covered. They need warmth and sun to germinate, so they'll wait for consistently warm days before sprouting. No fridge time needed.

If you go with seed packets: do the fridge stratification for 30 days first, then plant in spring after your last frost. Same shallow depth applies.

The guide mentions May as a general reference for colder Canadian climates. Your season starts earlier, so mid to late April works well for TN.

One thing worth knowing: milkweed is a perennial, so it usually won't bloom the first year, but once established it comes back every season and eventually draws in the monarchs.

Since the planting window has shifted with the season, you'd now be looking at next spring to plant, so no rush on the timing. You can browse our seeds and bombs here: https://lasclay.com/en/collections/garden

Warmly,
__
